common_name: Patata della Sila (Sila Plateau Potato IGP)

planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers 4 inches deep in cool, well-drained soil; this IGP designates several approved potato varieties grown together on Calabria's high Sila plateau at roughly 1,200m elevation.

directions: Patata della Sila is an IGP-protected potato grown on the volcanic and granite-derived, potassium-rich soils of Calabria's Sila National Park plateau, irrigated with cold mountain spring water and subject to wide day-night temperature swings that intensify flavor. Its yellow flesh carries above-average starch and dry matter, giving a sweet, buttery taste and excellent frying and roasting performance with good color retention. Hill soil around developing stems as the crop grows, and water consistently through tuber bulking, since the plateau's irrigation regime is central to the variety's character. Properly cured tubers store well in a dark, cool spot for up to eight months.

common_name: Vernaccia di Oristano (Sardinian Amber Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant grafted vines in spring in the sandy, saline-influenced alluvial soils of the Tirso river floodplain; needs a long, hot, dry Mediterranean season to develop its signature oxidative character.

directions: Vernaccia di Oristano is a genetically distinct white grape grown almost exclusively around Oristano in west-central Sardinia, unrelated to Tuscany's Vernaccia di San Gimignano despite the shared name. Its medium-small, waxy-skinned yellow-green berries are traditionally fermented and aged under a sherry-like surface veil of flor-adjacent yeasts, producing amber wines ranging from bone-dry to lusciously sweet, marked by toasted almond, dried apricot, and saline, honeyed notes. Train vines on sturdy trellising with moderate vigor control, since the variety's prized oxidative aromatics develop best under stress from heat and limited water rather than lush growing conditions. Today fewer than 50 hectares remain planted, making it one of Italy's rarest indigenous grapes.
sources: Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding & Jose Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes

planting.note: Plant grafted vines on well-drained limestone-hill slopes in spring; thrives in the warm, dry Planargia microclimate around Bosa on Sardinia's west coast.

directions: Malvasia di Bosa is grown on limestone hillsides around Bosa, Magomadas, Flussio, Suni, Tinnura, and Tresnuraghes in Sardinia's Oristano province, one of the rarest Malvasia clones under vine in Italy with roughly 8 hectares remaining. The wine made from it ranges from austere, bone-dry styles to lusciously sweet, fortified liquoroso bottlings, both marked by deep straw-to-amber color and aromas of honey, toasted almond, and dried fruit. Vines perform best with minimal irrigation once established, since the variety's concentrated, nutty character depends on heat and limited water rather than vigorous growth. Harvest at full ripeness in early autumn, and expect wines to gain further amber color and nutty depth with extended barrel or demijohn aging.
sources: Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding & Jose Vouillamoz — Wine Grapes

planting.note: Direct sow in late summer (late August to early September) along the Adriatic coast near Polignano a Mare; roots size up through autumn and winter for a December-to-March harvest.

directions: Carota di Polignano is a Puglian landrace carrot grown in the sandy coastal soil of the San Vito district near Polignano a Mare, where a single planting produces roots ranging unpredictably from pale yellow through orange to deep purple on the same bed. Roots reach 15-22 cm, and the variety is prized for high iodine uptake from its maritime growing site along with notably lower sugar content than modern orange carrots. Sow thickly and thin to final spacing once seedlings are established, since germination can be slow and uneven in this older landrace. Harvest through winter as needed, since roots hold well in the ground and sweeten further with cold exposure.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Carota di Polignano Presidium

common_name: Zafferano dell'Aquila (L'Aquila Saffron, Piano di Navelli DOP)

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in sharply drained, well-structured soil in late summer in the Navelli Valley's 700-900m elevation plain; registered in Italy's National Seed Register as Crocus sativus cv Piano di Navelli.

directions: Zafferano dell'Aquila has been grown for over 600 years on the Navelli plain near L'Aquila in Abruzzo, where a DOP-protected strain is agronomically distinct from saffron grown in other Italian regions, prized for unusually high safranal content, pungent aroma, and intense coloring strength. The lilac-purple autumn flowers must be picked at dawn and the three crimson stigmas plucked and dried the same day to preserve their aromatic compounds. The valley's rich, well-drained soil, mild summers, and rainy springs produce larger corms and longer stigmas than typical commercial saffron. Lift and divide overcrowded corm clusters every three to four years to maintain flowering vigor.
sources: Istituto Nazionale di Ricerca per gli Alimenti e la Nutrizione

common_name: Lenticchia di Santo Stefano di Sessanio (Gran Sasso Mountain Lentil)

planting.note: Direct sow in March on high mountain plots once soil is workable; traditionally grown above 1,200m in the Gran Sasso foothills of Abruzzo, with harvest delayed by altitude into midsummer.

directions: This Slow Food Presidium lentil has been grown since at least the Middle Ages on small, thin-soiled mountain plots around Santo Stefano di Sessanio in Abruzzo's Gran Sasso range, at elevations exceeding 1,200 meters. The seeds are notably tiny, only 2-5 mm across, flattened and rounded, and a dark brownish-purple color distinctly deeper than common lentils, with an earthy, nutty flavor and delicate fragrance. Their small size and thin seed coat mean they need no presoaking before cooking and cook quickly compared to larger lentil types. Sow directly in poor, stony, well-drained soil in spring, since the plant's resilience to thin mountain soils and short growing windows is central to the landrace's character, and harvest by hand in mid-to-late summer once pods dry on the plant.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Lenticchia di Santo Stefano di Sessanio Presidium

common_name: Aglio Rosso di Sulmona (Sulmona Red Garlic)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves in November on the Conca di Sulmona plateau in Abruzzo's Peligna Valley; overwinters as a hardy bulb and bulbs up through the following summer for a June-July harvest.

directions: Aglio Rosso di Sulmona is a small-headed hardneck-type garlic landrace from the Peligna Valley around Sulmona in Abruzzo, long listed on Slow Food's Ark of Taste, distinguished by white bulb wrappers surrounding vividly red-violet cloves. Despite its diminutive size compared to common garlic, it carries an unusually high concentration of essential oils, giving a pungent yet sweet flavor strong enough that a single clove can season a whole dish. Plant cloves root-down in fertile, well-drained valley soil in late autumn, and the crop is traditionally harvested and braided into long strings for curing and storage rather than simply bunched. Allow foliage to die back naturally before lifting to maximize bulb flavor and storage life.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Aglio Rosso di Sulmona Ark of Taste entry

common_name: Opperdoezer Ronde (Dutch Heirloom Early Potato PDO)

planting.note: Plant seed tubers in the sandy, barren soils typical of the Opperdoes polder in North Holland; an early, short-season type bulking up over just 10-12 weeks.

directions: First grown in 1860 in the village of Opperdoes in North Holland and EU-protected since 1996, Opperdoezer Ronde is a small, early, waxy potato with a slightly irregular oval shape, pitted eyes, thin delicate skin, and pale yellow-white flesh. Its low starch content and distinct earthy sweetness come partly from the lean, sandy, saline-influenced polder soil of its home region, which cannot be replicated elsewhere. Plant in loose, well-drained soil and hill lightly as shoots emerge; because the variety matures quickly, an early planting right around last frost gives the longest harvest window before summer heat sets in. Harvest as soon as tubers reach a usable size, since the thin skins make this a fresh, short-storage potato best enjoyed boiled or steamed rather than held long-term.
sources: Wageningen University & Research — PDO Opperdoezer Potatoes in the Netherlands

common_name: Westlandse Druif (Westland Greenhouse Table Grape PGI)

planting.note: Plant in a heated glasshouse or large sun-room trained on standing trellis wires; the Dutch Westland tradition grows this grape entirely under glass since it cannot tolerate outdoor cultivation in the Netherlands' damp climate.

directions: Westlandse Druif is a PGI-protected greenhouse table grape tradition from the Westland glasshouse district of South Holland, covering several dessert grape types grown entirely under glass to escape the region's cool, humid outdoor climate and chronic mildew pressure. Vines produce large bunches, averaging around 500 grams but ranging from 300 to over 1,200 grams, of round-to-oval, waxy-skinned berries in colors from deep blue to pale green-white depending on the variety grown. All work, from hand-thinning bunches roughly two months before ripening to harvest, is done by hand to maximize size, shelf life, and quality. Growers can heat the glasshouse to force an early June crop or let it ripen unforced into August, a flexibility unique to this indoor growing method.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Westlandse Tafeldruiven Ark of Taste entry
